claim: FUNDC1 is a mitophagy receptor that plays a critical role in EPO-driven erythropoiesis induced by stresses.
source: In this study, we showed that FUNDC1, a mitophagy receptor, plays a critical role in EPO-driven erythropoiesis induced by stresses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: EPO production is impaired in REPs in Fundc1-/- mice upon stresses.
source: Mechanistically, EPO production is impaired in REPs in Fundc1-/- mice upon stresses, and the impairment is caused by the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, which consequently leads to the elevation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS) level and triggers inflammatory responses by up-regulating proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a mechanistic finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The impairment of EPO production in Fundc1-/- mice is caused by the accumulation of damaged mitochondria.
source: Mechanistically, EPO production is impaired in REPs in Fundc1-/- mice upon stresses, and the impairment is caused by the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, which consequently leads to the elevation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS) level and triggers inflammatory responses by up-regulating proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This causal relationship is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Accumulation of damaged mitochondria leads to elevation of ROS levels in REPs.
source: Mechanistically, EPO production is impaired in REPs in Fundc1-/- mice upon stresses, and the impairment is caused by the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, which consequently leads to the elevation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS) level and triggers inflammatory responses by up-regulating proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements of ROS levels in the results section.

claim: Elevated ROS levels trigger inflammatory responses by up-regulating proinflammatory cytokines.
source: Mechanistically, EPO production is impaired in REPs in Fundc1-/- mice upon stresses, and the impairment is caused by the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, which consequently leads to the elevation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS) level and triggers inflammatory responses by up-regulating proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This mechanistic link is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements of inflammatory cytokines in the results.

claim: Inflammatory factors promote the myofibroblastic transformation of REPs.
source: These inflammatory factors promote the myofibroblastic transformation of REPs, resulting in the reduction of EPO production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence data showing α-SMA expression in REPs.

claim: Myofibroblastic transformation of REPs results in the reduction of EPO production.
source: These inflammatory factors promote the myofibroblastic transformation of REPs, resulting in the reduction of EPO production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EPO measurements in transformed REPs.

claim: Erythropoiesis is a highly dynamic and tightly regulated process in which red blood cells are generated from immature progenitors in the bone marrow.
source: Erythropoiesis is a highly dynamic and tightly regulated process in which red blood cells are generated from immature progenitors in the bone marrow (An et al., 2015; Nandakumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Erythropoiesis is mainly driven by the cytokine glycoprotein erythropoietin (EPO).
source: This process is mainly driven by the cytokine glycoprotein erythropoietin (EPO) (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Upon engagement of EPO with EPOR, the JAK-STAT pathway is activated to prevent committed erythroid progenitors from apoptosis and to facilitate their proliferation and differentiation into red blood cells.
source: Upon the engagement of EPO with its receptor, erythropoietin receptor (EPOR), the Janus kinase (JAK) signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway is activated to prevent committed erythroid progenitors from apoptosis and to facilitate their proliferation and differentiation into red blood cells (Nandakumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EPO signaling, supported by a citation.

claim: During the final maturation step of erythropoiesis, reticulocytes need to remove all of the remaining organelles, including mitochondria, endocytic vesicles, ribosomes, Golgi cisternae, and endoplasmic reticulum.
source: During the final maturation step of erythropoiesis, reticulocytes need to remove all of the remaining organelles, including mitochondria, endocytic vesicles, ribosomes, Golgi cisternae, and endoplasmic reticulum (Koury et al., 2005; Gronowicz et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about reticulocyte maturation, supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondria are the most abundant organelles for removal during reticulocyte maturation.
source: Among them, mitochondria are the most abundant organelles for removal (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by a citation.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial removal are linked to the dysfunction of red blood cells and can lead to anemia.
source: Prior studies have demonstrated that defects in mitochondrial removal are linked to the dysfunction of red blood cells and can lead to anemia (Kundu et al., 2008; Mortensen et al., 2010; Honda et al., 2014; Nishida et al., 2009; Schweers et al., 2007; Sandoval et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: EPO is primarily secreted by the kidneys during adulthood by the renal EPO-producing cells (REPs) located in the renal cortex and outer medulla.
source: As one of the key regulators of erythropoiesis, EPO is primarily secreted by the kidneys during adulthood by the renal EPO-producing cells (REPs) located in the renal cortex and outer medulla (Pan et al., 2011; Yamazaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EPO production, supported by citations.

claim: REPs possess functional plasticity for EPO production in response to hypoxia and other microenvironmental changes.
source: REPs possess functional plasticity for EPO production in response to hypoxia and other microenvironmental changes (Souma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Hypoxic stresses stabilize hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), especially HIF2α, which binds to the enhancer region of HIF binding element of the EPO gene and upregulates its expression.
source: For instance, hypoxic stresses stabilize hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), especially HIF2α, which binds to the enhancer region of HIF binding element of the EPO gene and upregulates its expression (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hypoxic regulation of EPO, supported by a citation.

claim: Proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNFa and IL1b, promote the myofibroblastic transition of REPs.
source: Upon inflammation or with chronic diseases, however, proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNFa and IL1b, promote the myofibroblastic transition of REPs (Asada et al., 2011), concomitantly repress EPO production in REPs (Frede et al., 1997), and ultimately lead to anemia (Weiss and Goodnough, 2005; Guo et al., 1999; Inoue et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Proinflammatory cytokines repress EPO production in REPs.
source: Upon inflammation or with chronic diseases, however, proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNFa and IL1b, promote the myofibroblastic transition of REPs (Asada et al., 2011), concomitantly repress EPO production in REPs (Frede et al., 1997), and ultimately lead to anemia (Weiss and Goodnough, 2005; Guo et al., 1999; Inoue et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondrial quality control exerts protective roles in a variety of renal disorders.
source: Although mitochondrial quality control exerts protective roles in a variety of renal disorders (Liu et al., 2014), whether and how it might be implicated in REPs during chronic or inflammatory diseases remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Mitochondria are essential organelles that maintain cellular energy and redox homeostasis and are the major source and target of intracellular oxidative stress.
source: Mitochondria are essential organelles that maintain cellular energy and redox homeostasis and are the major source and target of intracellular oxidative stress (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial function, supported by a citation.

claim: Mitochondria play central roles in regulating innate immunity and apoptosis.
source: They also play central roles in regulating innate immunity and apoptosis (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial function, supported by a citation.

claim: Mitophagy is the major mechanism sustaining mitochondrial homeostasis and quality control.
source: Mitophagy, a selective type of autophagy that allows the elimination of unwanted or damaged mitochondria, is the major mechanism sustaining mitochondrial homeostasis and quality control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitophagy, supported by the context and citations in the paragraph.

claim: Mitophagy can be mediated by the PINK1-PRKN pathway and/or by mitophagic receptors residing in the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Mitophagy can be mediated by the PTEN-induced putative kinase 1-Parkin (PINK1-PAKN) pathway and/or by mitophagic receptors residing in the outer mitochondrial membrane (Wei et al., 2015; Wu and Chen, 2015), such as BCL2 Interacting Protein 3 Like (BNIP3L, also named as NIX) (Novak et al., 2010), BCL2 interacting protein 3 (BNIP3) (Hanna et al., 2012), FUN14 domain containing 1 (FUNDC1) (Liu et al., 2012a; Chen et al., 2014), Prohibitin2 (PHB2) (Wei et al., 2017), and FKBP Prolyl Isomerase 8 (FKBP8) (Saita et al., 2013) in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitophagy mechanisms, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Receptor-mediated mitophagy is important for erythroid maturation.
source: It has been demonstrated that receptor-mediated mitophagy is important for erythroid maturation (Kundu et al., 2008; Mortensen et al., 2010; Honda et al., 2014; Nishida et al., 2009; Schweers et al., 2007; Sandoval et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Bnip3l-/- mice exhibit anemia and reticulocytosis with defective mitophagy due to the persistence of the mitochondrial membrane potential and the resultant depolarization in the mitochondria.
source: For example, Bnip3l-/- mice exhibit anemia and reticulocytosis with defective mitophagy due to the persistence of the mitochondrial membrane potential and the resultant depolarization in the mitochondria (Schweers et al., 2007; Sandoval et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: In the reticulocytes of the Bnip3l-/- mice, mitochondrial removal still occurs, raising the possibility that additional factors are also required for mitochondrial degradation during red blood cell maturation.
source: However, in the reticulocytes of the Bnip3l-/- mice, mitochondrial removal still occurs, raising the possibility that additional factors are also required for mitochondrial degradation during red blood cell maturation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior studies that motivates the current investigation.

claim: FUNDC1 functions as a specific mitophagy receptor in response to mitochondrial stresses, such as hypoxia.
source: We have previously shown that FUNDC1 functions as a specific mitophagy receptor in response to mitochondrial stresses, such as hypoxia (Liu et al., 2012a; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior work by the authors, supported by citations to their previous publications.

claim: FUNDC1 regulates mitochondrial homeostasis, including mitochondrial fission and fusion, content alteration, quality surveillance and physical interactions with other organelles.
source: FUNDC1 regulates mitochondrial homeostasis, including mitochondrial fission and fusion, content alteration, quality surveillance and physical interactions with other organelles (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of Fundc1 results in the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and the activation of inflammasomes.
source: Deletion of Fundc1 results in the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and the activation of inflammasomes and is associated with a wide range of pathological conditions, such as hepatocarcinogenesis (Li et al., 2018) and heart failure (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Fundc1-/- mice exhibited comparable hemogram parameters of peripheral blood to WT littermates at 8–10 weeks old.
source: We found that in Fundc1-/- mice, the hemogram parameters of the peripheral blood, including erythroid parameters such as red blood cell (RBC) count, hemoglobin amount, hematocrit (HCT, measuring the volume percentage of red blood cells in whole blood), and reticulocytes, were comparable to those in the corresponding wild-type (WT) littermates at 8–10 weeks old (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Negligible mitochondrial accumulation was detected in the Fundc1-/- cells collected from the peripheral blood, spleen and bone marrow.
source: Despite evident mitochondrial retention in erythroid cells of Bnip3l-/- mice (Sandoval et al., 2008), negligible mitochondrial accumulation was detected in the Fundc1-/- cells collected from the peripheral blood, spleen and bone marrow (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Fundc1 deletion did not affect erythroid lineage commitment and differentiation.
source: In addition, Fundc1 deletion did not affect erythroid lineage commitment and differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), generation of hematopoietic stem and progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), or differentiation of other non-erythroid, hematopoietic lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H) in peripheral blood, spleen, and bone marrow, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FUNDC1 is dispensable for steady-state erythropoiesis and possibly for hematopoiesis.
source: Together, these observations suggest that FUNDC1 is dispensable for steady-state erythropoiesis and possibly for hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations presented in the preceding text.

claim: Fundc1-/- mice exhibited low survival with PHZ treatment compared to WT counterparts.
source: We found that when compared with WT counterparts, Fundc1-/- mice exhibited low survival with PHZ treatment (p = 0.04, n = 30) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PHZ-treated Fundc1-/- mice showed reduced RBC numbers, lower HGB levels, and decreased HCT values compared to controls.
source: Time-course hemogram examination showed reduced RBC numbers, lower HGB levels, and decreased HCT values in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice than those of controls (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no detectable difference in the maturation of reticulocytes between WT and Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Unexpectedly, there was no detectable difference in the maturation of reticulocytes between WT and Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The mitochondrial mass exhibited little difference between WT and Fundc1-/- mice during reticulocyte maturation.
source: Consistent with these findings, the mitochondrial mass, as measured with MitoTracker Green, exhibited little difference between WT and Fundc1-/- mice during reticulocyte maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Fundc1-mediated mitophagy is dispensable for reticulocyte maturation.
source: Thus, Fundc1-mediated mitophagy seems dispensable for reticulocyte maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about reticulocyte maturation.

claim: The total number of erythroid cells in the spleen of PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice was reduced compared to WT mice after 48 hr of treatment.
source: We found that the total number of erythroid cells in the spleen of PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice was reduced compared to WT mice after 48 hr of treatment (p<0.05, Figure 1D), while there were no apparent differences in spleen size, weight, and color (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was a transient reduction of the R2 population (CD71hiTer119+) in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Subsequent analysis revealed a transient reduction of the erythroid compartment such as the R2 population (CD71hiTer119+) (mean 8% vs 2%, p<0.01) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study, supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The decreased R2 population was unlikely to be due to elevated apoptosis.
source: Nonetheless, the decreased R2 population was unlikely to be due to elevated apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G), accumulation of mitochondrial mass (Figure 1G), aberrant mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 1H), or enhanced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) level (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing no significant differences in apoptosis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy is dispensable for steady-state erythropoiesis, whereas it is involved in PHZ-induced stress erythropoiesis.
source: Together, our results suggest that FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy is dispensable for steady-state erythropoiesis, whereas it is involved in PHZ-induced stress erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental observations in the section.

claim: The JAK-STAT signaling pathway was among the top five significantly enriched pathways in differentially expressed genes in Fundc1-/- R2 cells.
source: We found that the JAK-STAT signaling pathway was among the top five significantly enriched pathways (Figure 2B), in agreement with gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 2C) and gene set quantitative analysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct finding from transcriptome analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Key components and downstream targets of JAK-STAT signaling pathway, such as Crebbp, Ep300, Irf9, and Spred2, were downregulated in Fundc1-/- R2 cells.
source: The key components and downstream targets of JAK-STAT signaling pathway, such as Crebbp, Ep300, Irf9, and Spred2, were also downregulated in Fundc1-/- R2 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct finding from transcriptome analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The levels of phosphorylated STAT5 and STAT3 were significantly lower in PHZ-Fundc1-/- R2 cells than those in the WT counterparts.
source: In striking contrast, the levels of phosphorylation of STAT5 and STAT3 were significantly lower in PHZ-Fundc1-/- R2 cells than those in the WT counterparts (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The JAK-STAT signaling pathway is hypoactivated in PHZ-treated Fundc1-/- R2 cells.
source: Thus, the JAK-STAT signaling pathway is hypoactivated in PHZ-treated Fundc1-/- R2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation data of STAT proteins.

claim: Fundc1 deletion had no apparent effect on Epor expression in R2 cells.
source: We then investigated the Epor expression in R2 cells in WT and Fundc1-/- mice with or without PHZ treatment and found no apparent changes when Fundc1 was deleted (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The serum EPO level was significantly reduced in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice compared with the corresponding controls.
source: However, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) experiments showed that the serum EPO level was significantly reduced in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice compared with the corresponding controls (6,100 vs 4,400 and 4,500 vs 3,500 pg/mL after 24 and 48 hr of PHZ treatment, respectively, p<0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from ELISA measurements, supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Exogenous administration of EPO to PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice restored peripheral RBC number and HGB level to levels comparable with WT counterparts.
source: More importantly, exogenous administration of EPO (1,000 IU/kg) to PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 2J) showed the comparable peripheral RBC number and HGB level with their WT counterparts (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from EPO supplementation experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Erythroid differentiation in the spleen of PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice was restored to the levels of PHZ-WT controls after EPO administration.
source: Erythroid differentiation in the spleen of PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice was restored to the levels of PHZ-WT controls (particularly of R2) as well (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis after EPO supplementation, supported by data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Insufficient EPO supply underlies the reduced RBC number in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: These results suggested that insufficient EPO supply underlies the reduced RBC number in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EPO supplementation rescue experiments.

claim: No difference in EPO production was observed between Fundc1-/- mice and the control mice in the pure anemic model determined via phlebotomy.
source: In contrast, no difference in EPO production was observed between Fundc1-/- mice and the control mice in the pure anemic model as determined via phlebotomy of 500 μL blood for three consecutive days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G), suggesting that the reduced EPO production in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice most likely arises from the oxidative stress of PHZ.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from phlebotomy experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: Fundc1 is highly and ubiquitously expressed in the kidney.
source: We found that Fundc1 was highly and ubiquitously expressed in the kidney (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The mRNA level of Epo in kidney of Fundc1-/- mice was significantly lower than that of WT counterparts at 48 hr after PHZ treatment.
source: In addition, the mRNA level of Epo in kidney of Fundc1-/- mice was indeed significantly lower than that of its WT counterparts at 48 hr after PHZ treatment (130 vs 61, p<0.05) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The expression of kidney injury markers Lcn2 and Kim1 was elevated in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We also detected the elevated expression of two kidney injury markers, Lipocalin-2 (Lcn2) (Moschen et al., 2017) and kidney injury molecule-1 (Kim1) (Humphreys et al., 2013; Figure 3B), although hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining illustrated no major structural alterations in the kidneys of PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HIF2α protein levels were similar between WT and Fundc1-/- kidneys after PHZ treatment.
source: Although HIF2α protein levels were sharply enhanced in kidneys of both WT and Fundc1-/- mice after PHZ treatment, the levels between WT and Fundc1-/- kidneys were similar (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction of EPO secretion is unlikely to be caused by the aberrant transcriptional regulation of Epo.
source: Thus, the reduction of EPO secretion is unlikely to be caused by the aberrant transcriptional regulation of Epo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HIF2α expression data showing no difference between WT and Fundc1-/- mice.

claim: PHZ treatment generally reduced the accumulation of total mitochondrial mass in kidneys.
source: In immunohistochemical analysis of mitochondrial membrane protein Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), we found that PHZ treatment generally reduced the accumulation of total mitochondrial mass (Figure 3D), suggesting that PHZ stress could promote the mitophagic process.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from immunohistochemistry, supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fundc1 deletion resulted in more retainment of mitochondria in the kidneys than in the WT controls after PHZ treatment.
source: In contrast, Fundc1 deletion resulted in more retainment of mitochondria in the kidneys than in the WT controls after PHZ treatment (Figure 3D), indicating that mitophagy was attenuated in Fundc1-/- kidneys under PHZ-induced stresses.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from immunohistochemistry, supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane proteins TIMM23, COXIV, and TOMM20 were more abundant in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells than in the control cells.
source: To further support this notion, we found that the mitochondrial membrane proteins TIMM23, COXIV, and TOMM20 were more abundant in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells than in the control cells (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Fundc1 deletion has little impact on mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: To distinguish between these two possibilities, we next examined mitochondrial biogenesis by determining the expression of the mitochondrial constitutive components of ATP synthase, including F1 subunit delta (Atp5d), nuclear respiratory factor 1 (Nrf1), and transcription factor A mitochondria (Tfam), and found no apparent differences between the kidneys of the PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice and the PHZ-treated control mice (Figure 3G). Thus, Fundc1 deletion has little impact on mitochondrial biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from qRT-PCR data showing no differences in mitochondrial biogenesis markers, supported by Figure 3G.

claim: The expression of autophagic proteins of LC3-II and P62 in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells was reduced.
source: Instead, the expression of autophagic proteins of LC3-II and P62 in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells was reduced (Figure 3E,F), suggesting that the accumulation of mitochondrial content is caused by defective autophagy.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The total level of mtDNA was elevated in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells.
source: With this aim, we removed the nuclei (to exclude the genomic DNA contamination) and mitochondria (to exclude intrinsic mitochondrial DNA contamination) (see Materials and methods) and discovered that the total level of mtDNA was elevated, while the cytosolic mtDNA was indeed induced in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis of mtDNA, supported by data shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Cytosolic mtDNA was induced in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells.
source: With this aim, we removed the nuclei (to exclude the genomic DNA contamination) and mitochondria (to exclude intrinsic mitochondrial DNA contamination) (see Materials and methods) and discovered that the total level of mtDNA was elevated, while the cytosolic mtDNA was indeed induced in PHZ-Fundc1-/- renal cells (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis of cytosolic mtDNA, supported by data shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Proinflammatory cytokines, including Il6, Tnfa, and Il1b, were significantly upregulated in PHZ-treated kidneys of Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Because cytosolic mtDNA acts as a critical trigger for cellular inflammatory responses (Allison, 2019), we then determined the level of inflammatory markers in renal cells and observed significant upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines, including Il6, Tnfa, and Il1b in PHZ-treated kidneys of Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Fundc1 deletion causes renal injury upon PHZ treatment by activating inflammation as a result of defective mitophagy.
source: Thus, Fundc1 deletion causes renal injury upon PHZ treatment by activating inflammation as a result of defective mitophagy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about mitophagy defects and inflammation.

claim: REPs exhibited stronger fibrotic signatures in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice than in the PHZ-WT controls.
source: We found that REPs exhibited stronger fibrotic signatures in PHZ-Fundc1-/- mice than in the PHZ-WT controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells exhibited more Epo production than PDGFRβ- cells.
source: As expected, PDGFRβ+ cells exhibited more Epo production (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In WT REPs, the levels of mitochondrial membrane proteins were sharply reduced upon hypoxic stress, concomitant with the enhanced conversion from LC3 I to II.
source: We found that in WT REPs, the levels of mitochondrial membrane proteins (TIMM23, COXIV, and TOMM20) were sharply reduced upon hypoxic stress, concomitant with the enhanced conversion from LC3 I to II, a hallmark of autophagy (Kabeya et al., 2000), indicating that hypoxia promotes the degradation of mitochondria by enhancing mitophagy (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting of cultured REPs, supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane proteins persisted at high levels in REPs of Fundc1-/- mice under hypoxic conditions when compared with the WT counterparts.
source: In contrast, these mitochondrial membrane proteins persisted at high levels in REPs of Fundc1-/- mice under hypoxic conditions when compared with the WT counterparts (Figure 4E,F), suggesting that mitophagy is impaired in REPs of Fundc1-/- mice under hypoxic stress.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting of cultured REPs, supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: PHZ induced the accumulation of mitochondrial mass in Fundc1-deleted REPs.
source: Similar to hypoxia, PHZ also induced the accumulation of mitochondrial mass as revealed by MitoTracker staining in Fundc1-deleted REPs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The fraction of mitochondria in the lysosome was lower in PHZ-mito-Keima/Fundc1-/- than in PHZ-mito-Keima/WT mice.
source: Although the fraction of mitochondria in the lysosome was elevated in PHZ-REPs from both mito-Keima/Fundc1-/- (34.1 vs 48.4%) and mito-Keima/WT (32.7 vs 35.8%) mice, the proportion of encapsulated mitochondria was lower in PHZ-mito-Keima/Fundc1-/- than in PHZ-mito-Keima/WT mice (48.4 vs 35.8%) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis of mito-Keima mice, supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Fundc1 deletion in REPs impairs mitophagy and results in the retention of a large number of damaged mitochondria under PHZ-induced stresses.
source: Thus, Fundc1 deletion in REPs impairs mitophagy and results in the retention of a large number of damaged mitochondria under PHZ-induced stresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mito-Keima experiments showing reduced mitophagy in Fundc1-/- REPs.

claim: A high dosage (100 μM) of PHZ markedly impaired mitophagy and reduced EPO expression in Fundc1-/- REPs when compared with their WT counterparts.
source: Although a low dosage of PHZ (10 μM) had little effect on mitophagy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C) and EPO production (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), a high dosage (100 μM) of PHZ markedly impaired mitophagy and reduced EPO expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) in Fundc1-/- REPs when compared with their WT counterparts.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from in vitro PHZ treatment experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The accumulation of mtDNA copy number was observed in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs.
source: Consistent with and likely the result of the retention of the damaged mitochondria, we observed the accumulation of mtDNA copy number, reduction of mitochondrial membrane potential, and elevation of mitochondrial ROS level in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Reduction of mitochondrial membrane potential was observed in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs.
source: Consistent with and likely the result of the retention of the damaged mitochondria, we observed the accumulation of mtDNA copy number, reduction of mitochondrial membrane potential, and elevation of mitochondrial ROS level in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from TMRM staining, supported by data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Elevation of mitochondrial ROS level was observed in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs.
source: Consistent with and likely the result of the retention of the damaged mitochondria, we observed the accumulation of mtDNA copy number, reduction of mitochondrial membrane potential, and elevation of mitochondrial ROS level in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from MitoSOX staining, supported by data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The level of proinflammatory cytokines, such as Il1b and Il6, was elevated in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs.
source: At the molecular level, the level of proinflammatory cytokines, such as Il1b and Il6, was elevated (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Epo production in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs was reduced.
source: Under such an inflammatory milieu, Epo production in PHZ-Fundc1-/- REPs was reduced (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy plays a protective role in REPs under stresses.
source: Thus, FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy plays a protective role in REPs under stresses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental observations about REPs in Fundc1-/- mice.

claim: Masson's trichrome staining of the renal sections from UUO-Fundc1-/- mice revealed more positive blue staining of collagenous fibers, indicating that renal fibrosis was exacerbated with Fundc1 ablation.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, Masson's trichrome staining of the renal sections from UUO-Fundc1-/- mice revealed more positive blue staining of collagenous fibers, indicating that renal fibrosis was exacerbated with Fundc1 ablation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from histological staining, supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fibrotic markers, such as Acta2 and Col1a1, were significantly upregulated in kidneys of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Consistently, fibrotic markers, such as Acta2 (encoding αSma) and collagen type 1 alpha one chain (Col1a1), were also significantly upregulated in kidneys of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice, while little difference was seen in the Fundc1-/- control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mitochondrial content was greatly reduced in kidneys of WT mice with UUO induction.
source: In addition, the mitochondrial content was greatly reduced in kidneys of WT mice with UUO induction, as revealed by immunoblotting analysis of the mitochondrial proteins of TOMM20, COXIV, TIMM23, and FUNDC1 itself (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mitochondrial elimination was partially blocked in the kidneys of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: In contrast, mitochondrial elimination was partially blocked in the kidneys of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Proinflammatory cytokines of Il6 and Il1b were upregulated in the UUO-Fundc1-/- renal cells.
source: Proinflammatory cytokines of Il6 and Il1b were upregulated in the UUO-Fundc1-/- renal cells, likely as a consequence of defective mitochondrial clearance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Fundc1 deletion induced an elevation of the mitochondrial ROS level in REPs of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We found that Fundc1 deletion induced an elevation of the mitochondrial ROS level (Figure 5F) and an alteration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 5G) in REPs of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice, with minor changes in mitochondrial mass (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Fundc1 deletion induced an alteration of the mitochondrial membrane potential in REPs of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We found that Fundc1 deletion induced an elevation of the mitochondrial ROS level (Figure 5F) and an alteration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 5G) in REPs of UUO-Fundc1-/- mice, with minor changes in mitochondrial mass (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Epo transcription was significantly impaired in Fundc1-/- mice in the UUO model.
source: As a result of the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria in REPs, Epo transcription was significantly impaired in Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: DNA methyltransferases Dnmt1, Dnmt3a, and Dnmt3b were upregulated in UUO-Fundc1-/- REPs when compared with their WT counterparts.
source: We found that these DNA methyltransferases were upregulated in UUO-Fundc1-/- REPs when compared with their WT counterparts (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice showed a fewer number of RBCs and lower HGB levels in the peripheral blood than cisplatin-treated WT mice.
source: We found that cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice showed a fewer number of RBCs, lower HGB levels in the peripheral blood (Figure 6B), and a lower serum EPO level (Figure 6C) than in cisplatin-treated WT mice.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from hemogram analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice showed a lower serum EPO level than cisplatin-treated WT mice.
source: We found that cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice showed a fewer number of RBCs, lower HGB levels in the peripheral blood (Figure 6B), and a lower serum EPO level (Figure 6C) than in cisplatin-treated WT mice.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from ELISA, supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Fundc1 ablation impaired the clearance of damaged mitochondria in the kidneys of cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Western blotting assay of mitochondrial membrane proteins (e.g. TOMM20 and COXIV) and autophagic proteins (e.g. P62, LC3II/I) revealed that Fundc1 ablation impaired the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Figure 6D) and caused elevated inflammatory signals (Figure 6E) in the kidneys of cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from western blotting, supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Fundc1 ablation caused elevated inflammatory signals in the kidneys of cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice.
source: Western blotting assay of mitochondrial membrane proteins (e.g. TOMM20 and COXIV) and autophagic proteins (e.g. P62, LC3II/I) revealed that Fundc1 ablation impaired the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Figure 6D) and caused elevated inflammatory signals (Figure 6E) in the kidneys of cisplatin-treated Fundc1-/- mice.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Deficient mitophagy was pronounced in REPs in cisplatin-treated mito-Keima/Fundc1-/- mice.
source: More importantly, deficient mitophagy was pronounced in REPs, as revealed by the direct assessment of the encapsulated mitochondria in PDGFRβ+ cells in cisplatin-treated mito-Keima/Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis of mito-Keima mice, supported by data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Increased mitochondrial mass was detected in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We also detected increased mitochondrial mass, dysregulated mitochondrial membrane potential (indicated by TMRM), and enhanced mitochondrial ROS levels in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Dysregulated mitochondrial membrane potential was detected in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We also detected increased mitochondrial mass, dysregulated mitochondrial membrane potential (indicated by TMRM), and enhanced mitochondrial ROS levels in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Enhanced mitochondrial ROS levels were detected in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: We also detected increased mitochondrial mass, dysregulated mitochondrial membrane potential (indicated by TMRM), and enhanced mitochondrial ROS levels in the PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Enhanced inflammation (e.g. Il6 and Tnfa) was found in PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: As a consequence of the abnormal mitophagy, enhanced inflammation (e.g. Il6 and Tnfa) and reduced EPO generation were found in PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6K,L).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Reduced EPO generation was found in PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice.
source: As a consequence of the abnormal mitophagy, enhanced inflammation (e.g. Il6 and Tnfa) and reduced EPO generation were found in PDGFRβ+ REPs in cisplatin-Fundc1-/- mice (Figure 6K,L).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from qRT-PCR analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Fundc1 deficiency impairs the clearance of damaged mitochondria and activates inflammation, which results in decreased EPO production in PDGFRβ+ REPs and aggravates the renal anemia.
source: Thus, Fundc1 deficiency impairs the clearance of damaged mitochondria and activates inflammation, which results in decreased EPO production in PDGFRβ+ REPs and, ultimately, aggravates the renal anemia (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental observations in the cisplatin model, supported by the model shown in Figure 6M.

claim: FUNDC1 is dispensable for the programmed mitochondrial elimination in the final step of erythroid maturation.
source: Additionally, it is somewhat surprising that FUNDC1 is dispensable for the programmed mitochondrial elimination in the final step of erythroid maturation, whereas another mitophagy receptor BNIP3L is required for the removal of mitochondria in reticulocytes during terminal erythroid differentiation (Schweers et al., 2007; Sandoval et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and comparison with prior literature.

claim: The function of FUNDC1 and BNIP3L is highly context- and cell-type dependent.
source: Thus, it appears that the function of FUNDC1 and BNIP3L is highly context- and cell-type dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the different roles of FUNDC1 and BNIP3L in different cellular contexts.

claim: The expression of HIF2α is largely unaffected by Fundc1 deletion.
source: In this study, we found that the expression of HIF2α is largely unaffected by Fundc1 deletion, indicating that reduced EPO production in Fundc1-/- mice is likely to be unrelated to the oxygen-sensing mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about HIF2α expression.

claim: The low yield of EPO may be due to the reduced number of REPs and/or compromised function during REP transformation to myofibroblasts.
source: Instead, the low yield of EPO may be due to the reduced number of REPs and/or compromised function during REP transformation to myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: The fraction of PDGFRβ+ REPs is unchanged in Fundc1-/- mice when compared with the WT controls under stresses.
source: Nonetheless, we found that the fraction of PDGFRβ+ REPs is unchanged in Fundc1-/- mice when compared with the WT controls under stresses (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation, though the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in the mitochondrial ROS levels, as a result of defective mitophagy, provokes inflammatory responses in REPs.
source: However, in the purified REPs from Fundc1-/- mice, we showed that the increase in the mitochondrial ROS levels, as a result of defective mitophagy, provokes inflammatory responses, including the upregulation of TNFa, IL6 and IL1b in REPs, and subsequently lead to fibrotic transformation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about ROS and inflammation.

claim: Activation of inflammatory signals, such as NFκB, TNFa, IL1b, and IL6, repress EPO production in REPs and promote their transition to myofibroblasts.
source: Although prior studies demonstrated that activation of inflammatory signals, such as NFκB (Souma et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012b), TNFa (Frede et al., 1997), IL1b (Frede et al., 1997), IL6 (Stenvinkel et al., 2005), repress EPO production in REPs and promote their transition to myofibroblasts (Guo et al., 1999; Inoue et al., 2010; Souma et al., 2013; Ernandez and Mayadas, 2009), in this study we provide the first link between deficient mitophagy and EPO production in REPs with the induction of inflammation as the intermediate step.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: This study provides the first link between deficient mitophagy and EPO production in REPs with the induction of inflammation as the intermediate step.
source: Although prior studies demonstrated that activation of inflammatory signals, such as NFκB (Souma et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012b), TNFa (Frede et al., 1997), IL1b (Frede et al., 1997), IL6 (Stenvinkel et al., 2005), repress EPO production in REPs and promote their transition to myofibroblasts (Guo et al., 1999; Inoue et al., 2010; Souma et al., 2013; Ernandez and Mayadas, 2009), in this study we provide the first link between deficient mitophagy and EPO production in REPs with the induction of inflammation as the intermediate step.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: Mitophagy represents an essential element of mitochondrial quality control in response to renal injury or anemia caused by UUO, PHZ, or cisplatin.
source: Therefore, by selectively removing the damaged mitochondria, mitophagy represents an essential element of mitochondrial quality control in response to renal injury or anemia caused by UUO, PHZ, or cisplatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations across multiple disease models.

claim: Defective mitophagy might result in metabolic reprogramming, which is widely observed in renal epithelial cells or myofibroblast transformation.
source: In addition, defective mitophagy might also result in metabolic reprogramming, which is widely observed in renal epithelial cells or myofibroblast transformation (Xu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2017; Livingston et al., 2019), and the alteration in mitochondrial metabolism may regulate EPO production epigenetically.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on prior literature and the current observations.

claim: The alteration in mitochondrial metabolism may regulate EPO production epigenetically.
source: In addition, defective mitophagy might also result in metabolic reprogramming, which is widely observed in renal epithelial cells or myofibroblast transformation (Xu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2017; Livingston et al., 2019), and the alteration in mitochondrial metabolism may regulate EPO production epigenetically.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observations about DNMTs and prior knowledge.

claim: Altered epigenetic modifications might be responsible for the reduced EPO production in Fundc1-/- REPs.
source: In line with this speculation, DNMTs, including DNMT1, DNMT3a, and DNMT3b, are upregulated, suggesting that altered epigenetic modifications might be responsible for the reduced EPO production in Fundc1-/- REPs, consistent with previous observations in mouse myofibroblast-transformed REPs (Souma et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016) and the cell lines generated from EPO-producing cells without the capabilities of EPO production (Yin and Blanchard, 2000; Steinmann et al., 2011; Sato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the DNMT expression data and prior literature.

claim: Myofibroblastic transformation of REPs causes REPs to lose their EPO-producing ability.
source: Myofibroblastic transformation of REPs, which causes REPs to lose their EPO-producing ability (Koury, 2014), is one of the major sources of myofibroblasts contributing to renal fibrosis (Souma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The kidney of Fundc1-/- mice displays a more severe fibrotic phenotype in UUO model.
source: In this study, we showed that the kidney of Fundc1-/- mice displays a more severe fibrotic phenotype in UUO model.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations from the UUO model.

claim: Receptor-mediated mitophagy protects against renal anemia and possible renal fibrosis.
source: Thus, receptor-mediated mitophagy protects against renal anemia and possible renal fibrosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Fundc1 is abundantly and widely expressed in the kidney.
source: In addition, we found that Fundc1 is abundantly and widely expressed in the kidney.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from expression analysis.

claim: FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy might play crucial roles in other types of renal cells besides REPs.
source: It is therefore highly likely that FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy might also play crucial roles in other types of renal cells besides REPs, and that these cells might also contribute to the death of Fundc1-/- mice under PHZ stresses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the widespread expression of Fundc1 in the kidney.

claim: FUNDC1-dependent mitophagy in tubule cells plays protective roles in ischemic acute kidney injury.
source: For example, during this study, it was reported that FUNDC1-dependent mitophagy in tubule cells plays protective roles in ischemic acute kidney injury (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study, supported by a citation.

claim: Targeting FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy should have pleiotropic therapeutic impacts in renal fibrosis.
source: It appears that targeting FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy should have pleiotropic therapeutic impacts by 'killing two birds with one stone'.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: Enhanced mitophagy might ameliorate anemia by attenuating inflammation in REPs in renal fibrosis.
source: In renal fibrosis, enhanced mitophagy might not only ameliorate anemia by attenuating inflammation in REPs, but also alleviate fibrosis by preserving and protecting the mitochondrial quality from other fibrogenic contributing cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about potential therapeutic mechanisms based on the study findings.

claim: Enhanced mitophagy might alleviate fibrosis by preserving and protecting the mitochondrial quality from other fibrogenic contributing cells.
source: In renal fibrosis, enhanced mitophagy might not only ameliorate anemia by attenuating inflammation in REPs, but also alleviate fibrosis by preserving and protecting the mitochondrial quality from other fibrogenic contributing cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about potential therapeutic mechanisms based on the study findings.
